axis: plainly noting a want of strength → dismissing a thing as too weak to count

members.tone: The flat baseline of the family - it names the missing physical strength and stops there, where every sharper member adds an attitude to the same fact.
Turns the missing vigor into something thin and drained, as though what is left had been diluted rather than merely reduced.
The British spelling, carrying the identical sting - vigor thinned out, not simply lessened.
Clinical in register, presenting the absence of energy as a condition to be observed rather than a failing to be scored.
Technical rather than evaluative - the want of vitality reads as a settled characteristic, not the temporary drain that *enervated* implies.
Implies vitality that was once there and has been taken away, so it asks for sympathy where *lame* asks for scorn.
The vitality has gone slack rather than been broken, leaving a limp, unstrung quality that *debilitated* renders as damage.
The mildest way of falling short - strength barely registering rather than failing, nearer to almost-nothing than to inadequacy.
Harsher than *faint* for the same shortfall - the lack sounds pitiable, and pity here shades into a verdict that it was never going to be enough.
Withering - the failure is not merely ineffective but embarrassing, contemptible for having been attempted at all.
The weakness is structural and imminent: the thing will give way under any real pressure.
Cooler and more formal than *flimsy* - there is simply not enough there to be solid, with no promise of collapse attached.
Damns the making rather than the thing - it says somebody rushed it or botched it, and the word will not let that go.
Of light, it reports thin brightness plainly, without the sickliness *pallid* or the melancholy *wan* brings to the same dimness.
Makes the dim light sound drained and washed out, an unwell version of what *pale* states neutrally.
The weak light sounds dispirited, a dimness with something melancholy in it that *pale* would only measure.
